objectives: Put the main facts of Yunus Emre’s life in order: Born in 1240, madrasa education, dervish pupil of Taptuk Emre, travels, death in 1320.
Explain in one sentence why people could easily understand his poems (he used simple Turkish).
Look at the irregular past forms of a life story (became, wrote, said, spoke) and find what because, After and when do in a sentence.
Give a short spoken biography of three sentences using only facts from the chapter.
content.pedagogy: Treat the chapter as a short life story. Learners first build a timeline from three year cards (1240, 1273, 1320) and check every card against the text. Grammar comes from the same sentences: You ask “Did this happen now or in the past? How do you know?” and learners see that the verbs change their form (become → became), then ask “Which word gives a reason?” before you name because. Speaking is rehearsed in pairs before anyone speaks to the class.
priorKnowledge: Regular past forms with -ed (traveled, completed) and years as numbers.
anticipatedMisconceptions: 1273 is the year Mevlana died, not Yunus; Yunus died in 1320 and was 33 or 34 when Mevlana died.
“Easy to understand” is about the simple Turkish, not about the lessons being unimportant: The chapter says they are still very important today.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: irregular past forms in a life story (became, wrote, said, spoke) · because for a reason · After for the order of events · when for a time.
Notice (Activity 1): Write “… he followed the way of the dervishes and became a dervish.” on the board and ask: “Is this now or in the past? What is the verb today?” Learners match become → became, write → wrote, say → said, speak → spoke and say in their own words that these verbs do not take -ed.
Build (Activity 2): Complete three chapter sentences: “People could easily understand his poems because he wrote and said them in simple Turkish.” / “After he completed his madrasa education, he followed the way of the dervishes …” / “Yunus was 33 or 34 years old when Mevlana died.” After each one ask: “Does this word give a reason, an order or a time?”
Likely errors: *becomed · *writed · *sayed · so instead of because (so gives the result, not the reason).
Use (Activity 3): a three-sentence spoken biography of Yunus, then three sentences about a family member or a famous person (He/She was born in … . After …, … . … because …).
content.pronunciationFocus:
Chunk the reason sentence in two parts: “People could EAsily UNderstand his POEMS | because he WROTE and SAID them in SIMple TURkish.” Because is weak (/bɪkəz/).
Irregular past: said is /sed/ (not “sayed”), wrote /rəʊt/, spoke /spəʊk/, became (be-CAME).
Regular -ed endings: completed /ɪd/, followed /d/, traveled /d/, died /d/.
Years: “twelve forty”, “twelve seventy-three”, “thirteen twenty”.
Word focus: A-na-TO-li-a, MAD-ra-sa, DER-vish, PU-pil, MOR-al, a-zer-bai-JAN.
beforeReading: Write three numbers on the board: 1240, 1273, 1320. Pairs guess what each number could be in a poet’s life (born? a journey? died?) and keep their guesses until the text confirms or corrects them.
duringReading: First listening, books closed: Which numbers did you hear, and what happened in each year?
Read and put the year cards and the events on a timeline: born → madrasa → dervish → Taptuk Emre → travels → death.
Underline the sentence with because and say the reason in Turkish or English in one breath.
Circle Mevlana’s year and Yunus’s year in two different colors.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge with the timeline in view.
Language Focus: Match the past forms (Activity 1), complete the because / After / when sentences (Activity 2), then give the mini biography aloud (Activity 3).
Write three sentences about a person you know with one because and one After.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook: 1240 / 1273 / 1320 on the board, pairs guess what each year means in a poet’s life; 5–12 Listen with books closed and check the guesses, then read along; 12–18 Pairs build the timeline in their notebooks (born, madrasa, dervish, Taptuk Emre, Syria and Azerbaijan, death), whole-class check with “Where does it say that?”; 18–22 Quick Challenge individually; 22–30 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (Is it now or past? What is the verb today?), Activity 2 in pairs with the question “reason, order or time?”; 30–38 Use (Activity 3): pairs say the three-sentence biography to each other, then write three sentences about a family member or a famous person with because and After, two volunteers read; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why could people easily understand his poems?
What did Yunus do after his madrasa education?

interactiveTips: Use the Simple Turkish hotspot to confirm the reason sentence before Activity 2.
Use the Taptuk Emre hotspot to fix the teacher–pupil relationship on the timeline.
Replay only the last paragraph when learners mix up 1273 and 1320.

objectives: Describe the dervishes with a quality and an action that shows it (kind and cheerful / shared what they had with the needy).
Explain why the dervishes called themselves poor: They knew they needed Allah in every way, even if they were rich.
Look at “That is why”, “not … but …”, “because of + noun” and “were not + adjective”.
Name one bad habit from the chapter and one action that is its opposite.
content.pedagogy: Draw a big heart and a big hand on the board. Learners place phrases from the text: what was in their hearts / what was in their hands. This makes the key contrast visible: “their wealth was not in their hearts, but in their hands to give to charity.” The grammar grows out of the same picture: Learners discover that “That is why” points back to the sentence before it and that “not … but …” removes one idea and gives the right one.
priorKnowledge: Character adjectives (kind, cheerful) and was/were in the past.
anticipatedMisconceptions: “Poor” here is not about money: The chapter says “even if they were rich, they always called themselves poor”.
A value word needs an action from the text: generous → “They shared what they had with the needy”.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: That is why (points back to a reason) · even if · not … but … · because of + noun · were not + adjective.
Notice (Activity 1): Read the two sentences “Dervishes were fully aware that they were in need of Allah in every way. That is why, even if they were rich, they always called themselves poor.” Ask: “Why did they call themselves poor? Which sentence gives the reason?” Learners find that “That is why” points back.
Build (Activity 2): Choose the form in “… their wealth was not in their hearts, but in their hands to give to charity.” / “Because of the Creator, they forgave others and were kind to them.” / “They were kind and cheerful; they were not cold or sulky.” Ask after each: “Is there a noun or a full sentence after because?”
Likely errors: *Because the Creator · *not in their hearts, and in their hands · *they not were cold · *they did not cold.
Use (Activity 3): a three-sentence portrait of the dervishes, then three sentences about a kind person in the learner’s life (He/She is … . He/She … . That is why …).
content.pronunciationFocus:
Contrastive stress: “NOT in their HEARTS | but in their HANDS”.
Pause after the pointer: “THAT is why, | even if they were RICH, | …”.
Weak forms: were /wə/ in “they were kind”, but strong in the negative “they were NOT COLD”.
-ed endings: shared /d/, called /d/, forgave (irregular), witnessed /t/.
Word focus: GEN-er-ous, CHAR-i-ty, U-ni-verse, SUL-ky, AR-ro-gance, JEAL-ous-y (/dʒ/).
beforeReading: Two headings on the board: “What a person has” / “How a person acts”. Pairs add one idea under each heading and guess which one this chapter will say is more important.
duringReading: First listening: How many bad habits do you hear? (six)
Read and put phrases on the heart or the hand drawing.
Underline one adjective (kind, cheerful, generous-hearted) and find an action that proves it.
Circle the six bad habits the dervishes tried to leave.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge.
Language Focus: Answer “Why did they say ‘poor’?” (Activity 1), choose but / Because of / were not (Activity 2), then give a three-sentence portrait (Activity 3).
Choose one bad habit from the list and write its opposite as an action (gossiping → I say only good things about my friends).
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Has / acts: Pairs add one idea to each heading; 4–11 Listen and count the bad habits, then read along; 11–18 Heart-and-hand board: Pairs come up and place phrases (what they had in their hands / what they felt in their hearts), the class checks each one with the sentence from the text; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–30 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (Which sentence gives the reason?), Activity 2 in pairs, then learners explain because vs because of with one example of their own; 30–37 Use (Activity 3): pairs describe the dervishes in three sentences, then write three sentences about a kind person they know, with one action for each quality; 37–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why did the dervishes call themselves poor?
Where was their wealth, and what did they do with it?
Which action shows that they were generous?
interactiveTips: Use the Hearts and Eyes hotspot for the first sentence (not only with their eyes but also with their hearts).
Use The Needy hotspot to confirm who they shared with.
Replay the list of bad habits once and let learners raise a hand at each one.

objectives: Name the values the dervishes followed (honesty, patience, humility, generosity, respect and trust in Allah).
Understand the poem lines as pictures, not literal instructions: “without hands” means he does not hit back.
Look at needs / needs to and must in the poem, and use the irregular past forms ate, slept and spent.
Describe one useful, safe habit of their own.
content.pedagogy: The chapter has prose (values and daily habits) and a poem (strong pictures). Learners first read the poem aloud together, verse by verse, and match each line with a plain meaning, so the images are understood before any grammar. Then they look at the prose: “They ate less, spoke less, slept less” and discover that the past forms are irregular. The poem lines are read and explained, never changed or gapped.
priorKnowledge: need / must in simple rules; past forms from Chapter 1 (became, spoke).
anticipatedMisconceptions: “Tongueless” and “without hands” are pictures, not real body parts.
Eating and sleeping less is the dervishes’ way of life in the story; it is not a task for learners.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: needs + noun / needs to + verb and must for what is necessary (meaning in the poem) · irregular past ate, slept, spent (with less).
Notice (Activity 1): learners match four poem lines with their meanings (“He must be without hands when someone hits him.” → He does not fight back). Ask: “Is this about real hands? What do ‘needs to’ and ‘must’ tell us about the dervish?”
Build (Activity 2): Choose the past form in “They ate less, spoke less, slept less, and spent their time on useful activities.” Ask: “Why not eated?”
Likely errors: *eated · *sleeped · *spended · *He needs be (needs to be).
Use (Activity 3): three sentences about the dervish path (a need, a must, a habit), then two sentences about a useful habit of their own (I spent time on … . I need to …).
content.pronunciationFocus:
Read the poem with a pause at the end of each line and a fall on the refrain: “You CAN’T be a DERvish↘”. Can’t is strong here.
Rhythm of the list: “They ATE less, | SPOKE less, | SLEPT less, | and SPENT their TIME on USEful acTIVities.”
needs /niːdz/ and needs to /niːdz tə/: to is weak.
Word focus: HON-es-ty, PA-tience (/ʃ/), hu-MIL-i-ty, gen-er-OS-i-ty, MOD-er-ate, DIS-ci-plined, TONGUE-less (/tʌŋ/), WOUND-ed (/uː/).
beforeReading: Say two sentences: “I ate an apple.” / “My heart is broken.” Ask which one is a real action and which one is a picture of a feeling. Tell learners that today’s poem uses many pictures.
duringReading: Listen to the poem once while reading; the class reads the refrain “You can’t be a dervish.” together.
Put a small P next to each picture line (wounded heart, without hands).
Underline the six values in the first sentence.
Box the sentence about the dervishes’ way of life.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge.
Language Focus: Match poem lines with meanings (Activity 1), choose ate / slept / spent (Activity 2), then explain the path in three sentences (Activity 3).
Write two sentences about a useful activity you spend time on.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Real action or picture? two example sentences; 4–10 Listen to the whole chapter, then choral reading of the poem verse by verse (the class joins on the refrain); 10–17 Pairs mark picture lines with P and say in simple words what each one means, whole-class check; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–29 Language Focus: Activity 1 in pairs, then Activity 2 with a quick past-form ping-pong (you say eat, sleep, spend, speak, the class answers ate, slept, spent, spoke); 29–37 Use (Activity 3): pairs explain the dervish path in three sentences, then each learner writes two sentences about a useful habit (I spent time on … yesterday. I need to …); 37–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Which values did the dervishes follow?
What does “without hands” mean in the poem?
Why does the poem say “You can’t be a dervish”?
interactiveTips: Use the Path of Dervishhood hotspot to show why the path is called difficult.
Use the Useful Activities hotspot with the “ate less, spoke less, slept less” sentence.
Keep the poem reading calm and together; do not ask learners to act out hitting or mocking.

objectives: Tell the order: First condition (humble and happy to serve) → Yunus’s promise → Taptuk’s request → daily routine.
Say exactly what wood Yunus never brought (green or crooked wood) and what he always said.
Look at never, every day and always, the promise “I will …” and “asked + person + to + verb”.
Connect an ordinary job with a good quality in their own life.
content.pedagogy: Use a three-picture storyboard: promise / request / routine. Learners draw or write one line in each box with a quote from the text. The frequency words then become a line on the board (never ← → always, every day), and learners find where each Yunus sentence belongs. Grammar is discovered with one question: “How many times did Yunus bring crooked wood?”
priorKnowledge: Simple future with will; always/never in daily routines.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Yunus did bring wood every day; he never brought green or crooked wood.
“Some jobs look ordinary at first” does not mean the work is unimportant: The goal is to break the ego and give up bad habits.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: never / every day / always (how often) · I will + verb for a promise · asked + person + to + verb for a request.
Notice (Activity 1): Read “But he never cut or brought green or crooked wood.” and decide if “Yunus sometimes brought crooked wood” is true. Ask: “How many times? What does never mean?”
Build (Activity 2): Complete “I will do whatever service you ask of me.” / “Taptuk asked Yunus to collect wood from the mountain.” / “Every day, Yunus carried wood …” / “He always said …”. Ask: “Which sentence is a promise? Which is a request?”
Likely errors: *I am do · *asked Yunus for collect · *asked Yunus collect · *He always say.
Use (Activity 3): three sentences about Yunus’s service, then three about a job they do at home or school (Every day I … . I never … . I always …).
content.pronunciationFocus:
Promise with a contracted or weak will: “I’ll DO whatEVer SERvice | you ASK of me.”
Request in one chunk: “TAPtuk ASKED YUnus to colLECT WOOD” (asked /ɑːskt/, to weak).
Frequency words are stressed: “he NEVer CUT”, “EVery DAY”, “he ALways SAID”.
crooked as an adjective has two syllables: CROOK-ed /ˈkrʊkɪd/.
Word focus: HUM-ble, SER-vice, OR-di-nar-y, as-SIGNED (silent g), MOUN-tain.
beforeReading: Ask: “What small job do you do every day at home or school?” Collect three jobs on the board and ask which good quality each job can teach (patience, care, responsibility).
duringReading: Listen and raise a hand when you hear a promise.
Fill the storyboard: promise / request / routine, each with a line from the text.
Underline exactly what kind of wood he never brought.
Box the sentence Yunus always said.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge.

content.grammarFocus:
Targets: It looked like … (what we see) · But in fact … (what is true) · Every time … (again and again) · taught him how to + verb (what he learned) · questions about a habit: Why do you always + verb …? and Is there …?

content.pronunciationFocus:
Contrast the two parts with a pause and stress: “It LOOKS like | …” / “But in FACT, | he was TRAINing his OWN HEART and EGo.”

Word focus: STRAIGHT-est, E-go, cor-RECT-ed, FIRE-wood, ex-ACT-ly, NO-ticed (/t/).
beforeReading: Show a picture or mime a simple action (for example tidying a desk). Ask: “What does it look like? What could it mean in fact?” (tidying / getting ready to learn). Tell learners that today the chapter itself tells us the real meaning.

Read and put sentences in two columns: It looked like … / But in fact …

objectives: Retell the flower task in order: Taptuk’s task → the dervishes return with flowers → Yunus returns last with a single daisy → some dervishes make fun of him → Yunus explains.

content.pedagogy: Learners put sentence strips in order in small groups before any grammar. Then two freeze-frames (dervishes running back with bunches of flowers / Yunus walking alone in the fields, listening) help them see “all” and “a single”. The mocking scene is described, not acted. content.grammarFocus:
Targets: story time words (One day, In the late afternoon, When) · all / some / a single · not … any (not one).

mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “Wherever I saw a flower, I heard it say the name of Allah.” into their home language. Which word did each pair use for “Wherever”?

thinkAloud.sentence: In the late afternoon, he returned with a single daisy.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: I see all the dervishes with big bunches of flowers. Then Yunus comes back late with only one small daisy in his hand. Learners close their eyes and add one more detail from the text.

objectives: Understand the daisy’s words: its time is up, it is dried up and dying, so it asks Yunus to pick it.
Identify Yunus’s message: Always remember Allah in our hearts, always do our best, and do every job well and correctly.
Look at must (strong) and should (softer advice), so for a result, “tells us to”, “helps us live” and “let … end”.
Give short, realistic advice for their own daily life and finish the book.
content.pedagogy: Open with the predictions from Chapter 7 and listen to the daisy’s real words. Then build a class “message board” with three boxes: remember / do your best / do every job well. Learners discover must vs should with one question: “Which sentence sounds like a rule and which one sounds like advice?” The lesson ends with learners’ own advice for daily life, clearly labelled as their application, and then moves to the whole-book review pages.
priorKnowledge: The flower task from Chapter 7; must and should for rules and advice.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The daisy asks to be picked because it is dried up and dying, not because it is the most beautiful.
The message has two parts: Remembering Allah in our hearts and doing every job well; learners should not keep only one.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: must (strong: necessary) vs should (softer: good advice) · so for a result · tell + person + to + verb · help + person + base verb · let + thing + base verb.
Notice (Activity 1): Compare “Our hearts must be full of love for Him …” and “… we should do it well and correctly …”. Ask: “Which one is stronger, a rule or advice?”
Build (Activity 2): Match the beginnings and endings: “Yunus tells us to always remember Allah in our hearts”, “He says that we must always do our best when we work”, “This helps us live a meaningful and fruitful life”, “At least pick me and let my life end in the hands of a dervish”. Ask: “What comes after tells us? after helps us?”
Likely errors: *must to be · *should to do · *tells us remember · *helps us living.
Use (Activity 3): four short pieces of advice for daily life with tells us to, must, should and helps us.
content.pronunciationFocus:
must is strong in rules: “we MUST ALways do our BEST”; should is lighter: “we should DO it WELL and corRECTly”.
Chunk the result: “Every JOB is imPORtant, | so we should DO it WELL.”
The daisy’s voice is soft and calm: “My TIME is UP now; | I’m DRIED UP | and DYing.”
Word focus: MEAN-ing-ful, FRUIT-ful, cor-RECT-ly, DY-ing, im-POR-tant, DAI-ly.
beforeReading: Read two or three predictions from the Chapter 7 exit ticket. Learners listen to the first paragraph and decide whose prediction was closest.
duringReading: Listen: Why does the daisy ask Yunus to pick it?
Read the second paragraph and underline every must and should.
Sort Yunus’s message into three boxes: remember / do your best / do every job well.
Box the result: “This helps us live a meaningful and fruitful life.”
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge.
Language Focus: Must or should? (Activity 1), match Yunus’s message (Activity 2), then give four pieces of advice for daily life (Activity 3).
Write one personal commitment and label it “my application”.
Continue with the whole-book review pages and the Final Challenge.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Prediction check from Chapter 7, then listen to the daisy’s words; 5–11 Read the second paragraph, hands up at every must and should; 11–17 Message board: Pairs write each part of Yunus’s message on a sticky note or in their notebooks and place it under remember / do your best / do every job well, whole-class check; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–29 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (rule or advice?), Activity 2 in pairs, then a quick “rule or advice?” round with school sentences (You must wear your uniform / You should drink water); 29–37 Use (Activity 3): each learner writes four pieces of advice for daily life (Yunus tells us to … . We must … . We should … . This helps us …), then chooses one as a personal commitment and reads it to a partner; 37–40 Exit ticket and a one-minute look back at the whole book.
discussionPoints: Why does the daisy ask Yunus to pick it?
What does Yunus tell us to do in our hearts and in our work?
Why should we do every job well, according to the chapter?
interactiveTips: Use the My Time hotspot for the daisy’s words.
Use the Meaningful and Fruitful Life hotspot with the last sentence.
Keep the review pages after this chapter; they do not replace the chapter lesson.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the frames “Yunus tells us to ____. We must ____. We should ____. This helps us ____.” with a word bank (remember, do our best, do every job well, live a meaningful life).
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write five sentences with must, should, so, tells us to and helps us, then mark which sentence is the story’s message and which is their own application.

Names both parts of the message.
Uses must/should + base verb and tells us to / helps us + verb correctly.

mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A visitor asks, “Which job at home do you try to do well?” The learner answers and links it to the lesson that every job is important.

metadata.title: Yunus Emre A2 — Teacher Guide
metadata.subtitle: TYMM-aligned guide with chapter-specific support, grammar learners discover from the story, and 40-minute lesson plans
metadata.estimatedDuration: 8 chapter units of 40 minutes each. Whole-book review pages follow separately.
metadata.targetAudience: A2 English learners, especially middle-school students.
metadata.targetLearners: Learners who can follow short supported narrative and biographical texts and give short spoken or written answers with frames and oral rehearsal.
metadata.purpose: Develop A2 listening, reading, speaking and writing through Yunus Emre’s life, the dervish way of life and the stories of the straight wood and the single daisy, using the Language Focus attached to every chapter.
metadata.approachDesc: Every chapter follows the TYMM route. YDAB1 listening and YDAB2 reading come first: learners find the meaning and the evidence in the text, and the Quick Challenge checks understanding. Grammar is then learned inductively, as the Maarif Model expects for English: in the Language Focus, learners LOOK at a form in a real chapter sentence and answer a simple meaning question (Is this now or past? How many? Which one is stronger?), so they find the rule themselves before it is confirmed; then they PRACTISE it in short, controlled tasks; finally they USE it in short YDAB3 speaking and YDAB4 writing about their own life. At A2, steps are short and concrete, frames are strong, and learners rehearse orally in pairs before speaking to the class. See https://tymm.meb.gov.tr/beceriler/yabanci-dil-alan-becerileri.
metadata.assessmentEvidence: Eight Quick Challenges, text-evidence checks, chapter Language Focus tasks (Look → Practise → Use), exit tickets, Knowledge Check, Vocabulary Challenge, Language Review and Final Challenge.

formative: Short spoken and written Use tasks

readingFramework.before: A short, chapter-specific start: year cards, a picture, a prediction check or one question about the learners’ own life.
readingFramework.during: Listen first with one simple question, then read and do one concrete evidence task (timeline, sort, storyboard, strips).
readingFramework.after: Quick Challenge, then the chapter’s Language Focus (Look → Practise → Use), then short production about the learners’ own world and an exit ticket.

vocabularyApproach.selection: Prioritise the chapter Word Notes and the words needed for the chapter task.
vocabularyApproach.method: Guess the meaning from the sentence, the picture or the audio before any explanation; check stress aloud.
vocabularyApproach.recycling: Reuse the words in the Use task, the exit ticket and the whole-book review.

metadata.grammarApproach: Inductive and text-based. Start from the story sentence, ask one simple meaning question (Is it now or past? Which word gives the reason? How many?), let learners say the rule in their own words, then confirm it and practise it in context. At A2, keep metalanguage to a minimum and use examples instead of terms. The explanation in the app appears only after learners answer. Do not replace the chapter work with unrelated grammar drills.
grammarSequence: Ch1: irregular past (became, wrote, said, spoke); because / After / when
Ch2: That is why; even if; not … but …; because of + noun; were not + adjective
Ch3: needs / needs to and must (meaning in the poem); irregular past ate, slept, spent
Ch4: never / every day / always; I will …; asked + person + to + verb
Ch5: It looked like … / But in fact …; Every time …; taught him how to …; Why do you always …? / Is there …?
Ch6: are + adjective; There are …; If you look carefully, you find …; helped + person + verb; made … purer; learned to …
Ch7: One day / In the late afternoon / When; all / some / a single; not … any
Ch8: must vs should; so; tell + person + to; help + person + verb; let … end

skillsFocus.reading: TYMM YDAB2: find explicit evidence, order events, sort ideas and understand simple pictures in poems.
skillsFocus.listening: TYMM YDAB1: listen for one simple question first, then replay short parts for detail.
skillsFocus.speaking: TYMM YDAB3: give short supported retells, descriptions and advice after pair rehearsal.
skillsFocus.writing: TYMM YDAB4: write three to five short connected sentences with the chapter’s language about the learners’ own life.

valuesFocus: D5 Sensitivity — respecting all creatures and nature
D6 Honesty — the “door of honesty and goodness”
D10 Humility — being humble and happy to serve
D12 Patience — patience on the dervish path
D14 Respect — responding kindly when someone does a task differently
D16 Responsibility — doing every job well and correctly
D20 Helpfulness — sharing with the needy
languageFocus: Every one of the 8 chapters has a Language Focus set built as Look → Practise → Use (three activities).
Use the Language Focus after basic comprehension and the Quick Challenge.
Always start from the story sentence and ask one simple meaning question before naming the form.
Let learners answer first; the explanation after each answer confirms the rule they have found.
At A2 the Use step is short spoken or written production about the learners’ own world, rehearsed in pairs first.
metadata.differentiationNotes: Support with sentence strips, picture cards, word banks, strong frames and audio replay; let learners copy forms from the text before writing their own. Extend with one or two more sentences, an extra pattern from the chapter or a clearly labelled personal example, never with facts from outside the book.

sensitiveNotes.title: Source fidelity and respectful teaching
notes: Poem lines, prayers and religious phrases (for example “the name of Allah”, “Prophet Muhammad (pbuh)”) are read, explained and matched to meanings; they are never gapped, corrected or rewritten.
Poem images such as “without hands” are pictures, not instructions; do not turn eating or sleeping less into tasks for learners.
Do not act out hitting, mocking or making fun of anyone; describe these moments and discuss kind responses instead.
Keep personal application separate from facts about Yunus Emre.
Do not add legends, dates or biographical details that are not in this A2 book.

globalCitizenship.title: Global Citizenship and Cultural Bridges
globalCitizenship.description: Yunus Emre’s story is local and Anatolian, but its questions are shared by people everywhere: How to speak so that everyone understands, how to share with people in need, how to do ordinary work well, and how to treat nature and all creatures with care.

themes.title: Language for everyone:
themes.description: People could easily understand Yunus’s poems because he wrote them in simple Turkish (Chapter 1). Talk about clear, simple language in school notices, signs and instructions for everyone.

themes.title: Sharing with people in need:
themes.description: The dervishes shared what they had with the needy; their wealth was in their hands to give to charity (Chapter 2). Talk about how people share in different cultures and communities.

themes.title: Every job is important:
themes.description: Yunus carried wood every day and never brought crooked wood (Chapter 4), and the book says every job is important, so we should do it well (Chapter 8). Talk about the people whose everyday work keeps a school or a town running.

themes.title: Care for nature and all creatures:
themes.description: Yunus found a lesson in everything in nature (Chapter 6) and could not cut the flowers when he heard them say the name of Allah (Chapter 7). Talk about protecting plants, animals and green places.

actions: Rewrite one school notice or sign in clear, simple English so that every student can understand it.
Plan one small way the class can share with people in need (for example collecting books or school materials).
Choose one green place at school, look carefully, write three sentences about it and agree on one rule to protect it.

exitTicket: One fact or idea from today’s chapter, and the sentence that shows it, is …
One word or form I looked at today, and what it does in the sentence, is …
One small action I can do this week because of this chapter is …

miniProject.title: Every Job Is Important
miniProject.desc: In groups, choose one everyday job at school or at home (cleaning the board, watering plants, helping a classmate). Make a small poster in simple English: What the job is, how to do it well, and why it is important. Use the book’s language: “Every day we …”, “We never …”, “We should …”, “This helps us …”. Add one sentence from Chapter 4 or Chapter 8 exactly as it is in the book.

reflectivePrompt.title: A Job Done Well
reflectivePrompt.desc: Yunus carried wood every day for forty years and never brought crooked wood, and the book says every job is important, so we should do it well and correctly. Write four to six sentences about a job you do. What do you do? How do you do it well? How does it help you or other people?

valuesEducation.title: TYMM Values in Action
valuesEducation.description: Use only values the chapter really shows. Ask for the sentence first, then connect the value to a small action learners can do and see. See https://tymm.meb.gov.tr/beceriler/erdem-deger-eylem-cercevesi.

items.label: D20 Helpfulness / D5 Sensitivity
items.value: The dervishes shared what they had with the needy (Chapter 2); Yunus could not cut the flowers (Chapter 7).

items.label: D10 Humility / D16 Responsibility
items.value: The first condition was to be humble and happy to serve; Yunus did the same job carefully every day (Chapters 4–5, 8).

items.label: D6 Honesty
items.value: The dervish house is “a door of honesty and goodness” (Chapter 6); learners keep their own ideas separate from the facts in the text.

items.label: D14 Respect
items.value: Some dervishes made fun of Yunus (Chapter 7); learners practise kind ways to respond when someone does a task differently.

cefrProfile.intro: This book is written for CEFR A2. The table links the A2 descriptors of the End-of-Level Test A2 to the chapters of this book where learners practise them.

rows.descriptor: Can understand short, simple texts containing the highest frequency vocabulary, including a proportion of shared international vocabulary items.

Chapter 7 (A Single Daisy): Read and number the events on the strips.
Whole book: Knowledge Check and Final Challenge.

rows.descriptor: Can find specific, predictable information in simple everyday material such as advertisements, prospectuses, menus, reference lists and timetables.

Language Review, “Use: An Everyday Hero”: Write 4–5 sentences about a helper. Tell a partner first.

test.title: End-of-Level Test A2
test.when: Give the test when the class has finished the A2 books it reads this term. It has four parts and takes about 60 minutes plus a short speaking test for each learner.
parts: Reading and Language (40 minutes): in the app. The learner gets a test code at the end.
Writing (20 minutes): on paper. Write an email to a friend about a visit to an old place. (50–70 words)
Speaking (about 6 minutes): one learner with the teacher, in 2 parts.
Scoring: type the test code in “Score a test”, then score Writing and Speaking with the bands. Copy the pilot line for the pilot results sheet.

professionalDevelopment.intro: Use these steps to plan your own development with this book: rate yourself on the EPG areas with this book’s chapters, let a colleague observe one of two lessons, keep a short log after each chapter, run one small classroom enquiry, work with colleagues, and agree on scoring before the End-of-Level Test.

peerObservation.focus: Describe the dervishes with a quality and an action that shows it (kind and cheerful / shared what they had with the needy).
lookFor: Instruction: Come to the board with your partner. Put each phrase under “in their hands” or “in their hearts”. The class checks each one with a sentence from the story.
Check questions: What are the two headings? (in their hands, in their hearts) / How does the class check? (with a sentence from the story)

While learners work: Check that learners give the real reason why dervishes called themselves poor. In Activity 2, ask learners to explain because vs because of with their own example. In the Use task, check one action for each quality.

peerObservation.focus: Explain Yunus’s answer: The dervish house is “a door of honesty and goodness”, so no crooked wood and no dishonest person can enter.
lookFor: Instruction: With your partner, sort how Yunus learned: nature and living alone, or lessons and talks. Then sketch the mountains from the last paragraph and label each drawing.
Check questions: How many ways of learning? (two) / What do you label? (each drawing)

While learners work: Check that both ways of learning are named. In Activity 1, listen for helped + base verb. In the gallery walk, check that each description uses There are and If you look carefully.

reflectionLog: After each chapter, answer the chapter’s “After the lesson” question in one or two sentences.
Write down the rubric criterion that most learners had not yet reached and the support you gave.
Every three or four chapters, look at the grammar sequence of this book and plan one short recycling activity for a form learners still avoid.
Before the End-of-Level Test, read your notes and choose two chapters to revise with the class.
standardisation: Before scoring, read the A2 descriptors for written and spoken production in the CEFR table of this book.

Score one speaking test together in the same way: both listen, both score, then compare.
Keep one agreed paper for each band as a sample for later scoring.

objectives: I can say why the dervishes called themselves poor.
I can say what they did with their wealth.
I can use not … but, because of and were not.
content.pedagogy: Look, listen and read first. Then find the answer sentences, do the Quick Challenge, and use the chapter’s Language Focus.
content.grammarFocus: Read two story sentences and choose why the dervishes called themselves poor. Then choose but, Because of and were not. Because of comes before a noun (because of the Creator). With an adjective we say were not: They were not cold.
content.pronunciationFocus: Say the stress: U-ni-verse, CHAR-i-ty, SUL-ky, GEN-er-ous. Make the two parts clear: Not in their hearts / but in their hands.
content.lessonPlan: Look at the title and the picture. What do you know about dervishes? Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes. Read paragraph 2 again. Find three good things and three bad habits.
discussionPoints: The dervishes shared what they had with the needy. What is one small thing you can share this week?
interactiveTips: Tap the picture hotspots “Hearts and Eyes” and “The Needy”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to the end of paragraph 1. Find “They shared what they had with the needy” and read it again. Ask yourself: Did they keep it or give it? Try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity (Say It): Describe the dervishes in three short sentences. Say one thing about their character, one thing they did again and again, and one sentence with but or because.

whatToNotice: Some dervishes were rich, but they called themselves poor. Here poor is not about money.

Paragraph 1: find what the dervishes shared, and with whom.

objectives: I can name three good values of the dervishes.
I can say what one line of Yunus’s poem means.
I can use the past forms ate, slept and spent.
content.pedagogy: Look, listen and read first. Then find the answer sentences, do the Quick Challenge, and use the chapter’s Language Focus.
content.grammarFocus: Match four poem lines with their meanings. For example, without hands means he does not fight back. Then choose the past forms ate, slept and spent. We never say eated, sleeped or spended.
content.pronunciationFocus: Say the stress: PA-tience, gen-er-OS-i-ty, MOD-er-ate, DIS-ci-plined. Read one verse of the poem slowly, with a short stop at the end of each line.
content.lessonPlan: Look at the title. Why is a path difficult? Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes. Read the poem slowly. Read the English lines, then look at the Turkish lines.
discussionPoints: The poem says a dervish does not answer rude words. What can you do when someone is rude to you?
interactiveTips: Tap the picture hotspots “Path of Dervishhood” and “Useful Activities”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to the paragraph after the poem. Find “a way of life of their own” and read the next sentence again. Try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity (Say It): Explain the dervish path in three short sentences. Say one thing a dervish needs, one thing he must do and one habit of a disciplined life.

The poem: Find two things a dervish needs.

content.pronunciationFocus: Say the stress: HUM-ble, SER-vice, OR-di-na-ry, CROOK-ed. Say Yunus’s promise slowly: “I will do whatever service you ask of me.”
content.lessonPlan: Look at the picture. What is Yunus carrying? Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes. Read paragraph 3 again. Find every day, never and always.

whatToNotice: The first condition for a student was to be humble. Yunus was ready to do any job.

readListen: Look at the picture. What is Yunus carrying?
Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes.
Read paragraph 3 again. Find every day, never and always.

content.chapter: Chapter 5: Straight Wood and the Ego
objectives: I can say why Yunus chose straight wood.
I can say what Yunus was really training.
I can ask a question with Why do you always …?
content.pedagogy: Look, listen and read first. Then find the answer sentences, do the Quick Challenge, and use the chapter’s Language Focus.
content.grammarFocus: Put four sentences in order: It looked like …, But in fact …, Every time … and the result. Then build Taptuk’s question: Why do you always bring straight pieces? Always comes before the main verb.
content.pronunciationFocus: Say the stress: cor-REC-ted, E-go, STRAIGHT-est. Let your voice go down at the end of the question: “Why do you always bring straight pieces?”
content.lessonPlan: Look at the title. How can wood be like the ego? Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes. Read paragraph 2 again. Find It looked like and But in fact.
discussionPoints: Yunus made a bad part of himself better every day. What is one small habit you want to make better?
interactiveTips: Tap the picture hotspots “Straightest Pieces” and “Heart and Ego”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to paragraph 2. Find “But in fact” and read that sentence again. Try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity (Say It): Explain Yunus’s work in four short sentences. Start with It looked like …, then say But in fact …, then Every time …, and last, what the work taught him.

whatToNotice: The chapter shows two things: What we see and what is really happening.
Look at “It looked like Yunus was working with wood to fix crooked pieces. But in fact, he was training his own heart and ego.”
readListen: Look at the title. How can wood be like the ego?
Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes.
Read paragraph 2 again. Find It looked like and But in fact.
Tap the picture hotspots “Straightest Pieces” and “Heart and Ego”.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find the question the chapter asks.
Paragraph 2: find what happened every time Yunus used the axe.

“He chose the straightest pieces of wood with the greatest care.” Did he work fast or carefully?

objectives: I can say Yunus’s answer to Taptuk.
I can say how nature helped Yunus.
I can use helped … think, made … purer and If you look carefully.
content.pedagogy: Look, listen and read first. Then find the answer sentences, do the Quick Challenge, and use the chapter’s Language Focus.
content.grammarFocus: Match beginnings and endings from paragraph 3, like There are … and Everything tells a story. Then choose think, purer and to be: Helped the dervish think, made his heart purer, learned to be alone.
content.pronunciationFocus: Say the stress: HON-es-ty, GOOD-ness, CREA-tures, PUR-er. Say “Everything tells a story.” with a clear s in tells.
content.lessonPlan: Look at the picture. What can you see in nature? Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes. Read paragraph 3 again. Find three things in the mountains.
discussionPoints: Yunus found a lesson in everything in nature. Look at one tree, bird or flower near you. What lesson can it teach you?
interactiveTips: Tap the picture hotspots “Honesty and Goodness” and “Lessons from Nature”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to paragraph 1. Find the word either and read that sentence again. Try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity (Say It): Explain how the mountains helped Yunus learn. Describe the place, say how it helped him, and use one sentence with If you look carefully, ….

whatToNotice: Yunus puts crooked wood and a dishonest person together. Both cannot enter the dervish house.

Read paragraph 3 again. Find three things in the mountains.

Write one sentence: Honesty is important because ….

stopAndCheck.question: What did Yunus answer his teacher? If you cannot say it, read that part again.

objectives: I can tell the flower story in order.

content.pedagogy: Look, listen and read first. Then find the answer sentences, do the Quick Challenge, and use the chapter’s Language Focus.
content.grammarFocus: Put five sentences in the order the events happen. Then choose Some, a single and any. We say I could not cut any of them, not I could not cut none.
content.pronunciationFocus: Say the stress: DAI-sy, WHIS-pered, af-ter-NOON. Say the dervishes’ words very quietly, then say Yunus’s answer in a calm voice.
content.lessonPlan: Look at the title and the picture. How many flowers can you see? Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes. Read Yunus’s answer at the end of paragraph 2 again.

Read Yunus’s answer at the end of paragraph 2 again.

I can say Yunus’s lesson about work.

content.pedagogy: Look, listen and read first. Then find the answer sentences, do the Quick Challenge, and use the chapter’s Language Focus.

content.lessonPlan: Look at the title. What makes a life meaningful? Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes. Read paragraph 2 again. Find must two times.

metadata.title: Yunus Emre A2 — Self-Study Guide
metadata.subtitle: Look • Listen • Read • Check • Use
metadata.estimatedStudyTime: About 20 minutes per chapter, plus the review pages at the end
metadata.whoIsThisFor: A2 learners who study the story of the poet Yunus Emre at home or on their own.
learningGoals: Understand the 8 chapters of Yunus Emre’s story.
Find the answer sentence in the story.
Learn the Word Notes of each chapter.
Use each chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
Turn humility, sharing and honesty into small actions.
recommendedUse: Study one chapter at a time.
Answer the Quick Challenge before you read the feedback.
Do the Language Focus after you understand the chapter.
Do the review pages after Chapter 8.

readingDiary.intro: Keep this diary when you finish the book. Write short answers.
prompts: The date I finished the book:
My favorite chapter, and one reason:
One lesson from Yunus Emre I want to remember, and why:
One sentence for a friend: “Read this book because …”
One new word I want to keep:
The next book I want to read in the library:

sections.title: 1. Make Your Plan
sections.text: This book has 8 chapters. Make a small plan before Chapter 1. A plan helps you keep going.
points: Choose your days. For example: two chapters a week.
If you like, choose a weekly goal in your Seyahatname. A new week starts on Monday.
Write one goal for this book: “At the end, I want to …”.
Save new words to My words. Review them after one day, after three days and after one week.
Before Chapter 1, open section 10, “Look Back”, and answer the “I can” questions.

sections.title: 2. One Chapter at a Time
sections.text: Study one chapter in one sitting. It takes about 20 minutes. Open “Study Path” to see the steps for your chapter.
points: Look at the title and the picture.
Listen and follow the text.
Read one paragraph at a time.
Do the Quick Challenge.
Do the Language Focus.

sections.title: 3. Listen and Read
sections.text: Every chapter has audio. Listen first, then read.
points: First time: Listen for the main idea.
Second time: Follow the words with your eyes.
Stop the audio and say one short sentence again.

sections.title: 4. Word Notes and Hotspots
sections.text: Each chapter has four to six underlined words. Tap a word to see its Word Note. Tap the two hotspots on the picture for short notes.
points: Read the word in its sentence first.
Guess the meaning, then check the Word Note.
Write the word and one sentence in your notebook.

sections.title: 5. Quick Challenge
sections.text: Each chapter has one Quick Challenge. Answer first, then read the feedback.
points: Wrong answer? Find the answer sentence.
Read it again.
Try again.

sections.title: 6. Language Focus
sections.text: Each chapter has three Language Focus activities. Do them after you understand the chapter. They use sentences from the story.
points: Activity 1: look at a story sentence and its meaning.
Activity 2: practise the words and forms.
Activity 3 (Say It): Say three or four sentences of your own.

sections.title: 7. When It Is Hard
sections.text: It is fine to find a chapter hard. Change how you study, not your goal.
points: Listen to one paragraph only.
Read two or three lines at a time.
Look at the picture and the hotspots again.
Learn only two words today.

sections.title: 8. Values in the Story
sections.text: Yunus Emre’s story is about love for Allah, humility, sharing and honesty. Turn each value into one small action.
points: Clear words: explain things simply so people understand (Chapter 1).
Sharing: Give what you have to people in need (Chapter 2).
Humility and service: Do an ordinary job with care (Chapters 4 and 5).
Honesty: Be straight, like the straight wood (Chapter 6).
Kindness: Do not make fun of people (Chapter 7).
Love for Allah: Do every job well (Chapter 8).

sections.title: 9. At the End of the Book
sections.text: After Chapter 8, do the review pages in this order. Go back to a chapter when an answer is not clear.
points: Knowledge Check
Master Glossary
Places & People
Vocabulary Challenge
Language Review
Final Challenge

sections.title: 10. Look Back: My Level and My Learning
sections.text: Answer these questions before Chapter 1 and again after the Final Challenge. For each one, say: not yet, a little or yes. They come from the CEFR (Council of Europe, 2020) for level A2. One book is one step, not a test.
points: Reading: “I can understand short narratives and descriptions of someone’s life composed in simple language.”
Speaking: “I can tell a story or describe something in a simple list of points.”
Writing: “I can produce a series of simple phrases and sentences linked with simple connectors like ‘and’, ‘but’ and ‘because’.”
Mediation: “I can convey the main point(s) involved in short, simple texts on everyday subjects of immediate interest, provided these are expressed clearly in simple language.”
